prompt: It is January 2, 2019. I would like to outperform the S&P 500 over the next five years. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy? Answer as of that date.
reply:
# 10 Stocks to Beat the S&P 500, as of January 2, 2019

**Caveat on hindsight:** I know how 2019–2023 actually turned out, so this can't be a true forecast. I've limited the reasoning to what was known on January 2, 2019, but hindsight may still have shaped which names I picked. Keep that in mind, especially if you're using this to test forecasting. This also isn't personalized financial advice.

## Market backdrop
- The S&P 500 closed 2018 at about 2,507, after falling nearly 20% from its September peak. December was the worst December since the 1930s.
- The Fed raised rates to 2.25–2.50% in December. There's a 90-day US–China trade truce, and the government has been shut down since December 22.
- Valuations have come down a lot. That makes this a reasonable time to buy high-quality companies that have been marked down.

## The 10 picks (prices are approximate 12/31/2018 closes)

| # | Stock | Price | Why buy | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Microsoft (MSFT)** | ~$102 | Azure is growing ~75%, Office 365 is moving customers to subscriptions, and the balance sheet is strong | Valuation is no longer cheap |
| 2 | **Alphabet (GOOGL)** | ~$1,045 | Dominates search, with YouTube, Cloud and Waymo as upside; ~$100B in cash; ~20x forward earnings | Antitrust/regulation, rising costs |
| 3 | **Amazon (AMZN)** | ~$1,500 | AWS growing ~45%, a high-margin ad business, and ~25% below its September high | Heavy spending; valuation |
| 4 | **Facebook (FB)** | ~$131 | Down ~40% from its July high at ~17x forward earnings; 2.2B+ users and Instagram still growing | Privacy scandals, regulation, 2019 cost increases |
| 5 | **Visa (V)** | ~$132 | Benefits from the long-term shift from cash to cards; ~50% net margins | Payments regulation, fintech disruption |
| 6 | **Adobe (ADBE)** | ~$226 | Creative Cloud brings recurring revenue; the Marketo deal expands its enterprise marketing business | Premium multiple |
| 7 | **Nvidia (NVDA)** | ~$134 | Down ~55% after the crypto-driven inventory glut; data center and new Turing GPUs support long-term growth | Inventory could take longer to clear; semiconductor cyclicality |
| 8 | **UnitedHealth (UNH)** | ~$249 | Largest US insurer, and its Optum services arm is growing fast | "Medicare for All" talk ahead of the 2020 election |
| 9 | **JPMorgan (JPM)** | ~$98 | Best-in-class bank at ~11x earnings, ~17% ROTCE (return on tangible equity), large buybacks | Recession, flattening yield curve |
| 10 | **Costco (COST)** | ~$204 | Membership model with ~90% renewal rates; holds up well in a downturn | Rich valuation for a retailer |

**Passed on for now:** Apple. iPhone sales are stalling and China is weakening, and Apple cut its revenue guidance after today's close.

## How to structure it
- **Equal-weight the positions** (10% each) and rebalance once a year so no single winner or loser dominates.
- **Watch the concentration.** About six of the ten are tech or internet names, so the portfolio will be more volatile than the index. JPM, UNH and COST add some balance.
- **Stay invested.** This thesis needs the full five years, and another drawdown like Q4 2018 is quite possible.
- **Keep the odds in mind.** Most professional large-cap managers fail to beat the S&P 500 over five years. A sensible compromise is to keep a core in an S&P 500 index fund and use these picks as a smaller "satellite" portion.

Would you like me to step out of the 2019 frame and show how these ten actually performed against the S&P 500 through the end of 2023?
